status: DRAFT v0.1: not yet reviewed, pretested or calibrated.
notes: Each action item names its cost. The climate belief item is reported separately and tested for whether it belongs on ENV. Nuclear and permitting are cross-cutting candidates.

items.subtopic: Level of climate action and its cost
items.stem: By when should the US aim to stop adding to the overall amount of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere (net zero)?
items.scope: Net zero means any emissions left are balanced by removing the same amount.

items.subtopic: Level of climate action and its cost
items.stem: How much more per month would you accept paying in energy costs for policies that fight climate change?
items.scope: Think of your own household's electricity and fuel bills.

items.stem: Should there be a federal tax on the carbon pollution from fossil fuels?
items.scope: A tax of $100 per ton would add about 90 cents to a gallon of gasoline.
options: Yes, a high and rising tax, around $100 a ton
Yes, a moderate tax, around $25 to $50 a ton

facts.claim: Burning a gallon of gasoline emits about 8.9 kg CO2, so $100/ton is about $0.89/gallon

items.stem: If there were a federal carbon tax, what should the money mainly be used for?
items.scope: Answer even if you oppose a carbon tax.
options: Equal rebates paid to every household
Cutting other taxes, such as income or payroll taxes

items.stem: Should imports from countries with weaker pollution rules pay a fee based on the carbon pollution from making them?
items.scope: Goods like steel, cement and aluminum.
options: Only if US producers also pay for their own carbon pollution

items.subtopic: Fossil fuel production on public land
items.stem: Should new oil and gas drilling be allowed on federal lands and in federal waters offshore?
items.scope: Land and waters owned by the federal government.
options: No new drilling, and phase out existing leases
No new leases, but existing ones can continue
Allow new drilling with strict environmental review
Expand drilling and speed up approvals

items.subtopic: Fossil fuel production on public land
items.stem: What should happen to coal-fired power plants?
items.scope: Plants that make electricity by burning coal.
options: Phase them out gradually as they age
Keep them running as long as they make economic sense
Use government help to keep plants open

items.stem: Should the US build more nuclear power plants?
items.scope: Plants that make electricity from nuclear energy.
options: No new plants, but keep existing ones running
Some new plants, under current safety rules
Many new plants, with faster approvals
items.notes: Cross-cutting candidate: support is high among both climate hawks and fossil-fuel supporters.

items.stem: Should government help pay to build new nuclear plants?
items.scope: Federal money, loans or tax credits.

items.stem: Should government require most new cars sold to be electric by a set date?
items.scope: New passenger cars and SUVs.
options: No requirement, but keep tightening pollution limits for new cars
No requirement and no tighter limits

items.stem: Should buyers of new electric vehicles get a federal tax credit?
items.scope: Credits for individual buyers.
items.context: There is currently no federal tax credit for buying an electric vehicle.
options: Yes, a smaller credit, only for lower- and middle-income buyers

facts.claim: Clean vehicle credit (IRC 30D) terminated for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025

items.stem: Which comes closer to your view?
items.scope: Think of industries like mining, oil and manufacturing.

sides.label: Protect the environment
sides.text: Stricter environmental rules, even if some jobs in those industries are lost.

sides.label: Protect the jobs
sides.text: Keep those jobs, even if the environment is less protected.

items.stem: For big projects like pipelines, power lines and solar farms, which comes closer to your view?
items.scope: Projects of any kind of energy.

sides.label: Thorough review
sides.text: Keep thorough environmental reviews, even if projects take many years to build.

sides.label: Build faster
sides.text: Speed up approvals, even if some environmental harms are missed.

items.notes: Cross-cutting candidate: clean-energy builders and fossil-fuel producers both favor speed.

items.stem: How much land should be protected from development like mining, drilling and logging?
items.scope: Land and waters in the US.
options: Much more, such as 30% of US land by 2030

items.stem: Should the federal government sell some of its land to states or private owners?
items.scope: Federal land such as national forests and grazing land, not national parks.
options: Only small parcels near towns, for housing

items.stem: Should the US take part in international agreements to cut greenhouse gas emissions, like the Paris Agreement?
items.scope: Agreements among most countries of the world.
items.context: The US is not currently part of the Paris Agreement.
options: Yes, with binding targets for each country
Yes, with voluntary targets, as in the Paris Agreement

facts.claim: US withdrawal from the Paris Agreement took effect in January 2026, one year after notification
facts.source: E&E News, 'So long, Paris: US officially leaves landmark climate pact' (Jan 2026); UNFCCC

items.stem: Which comes closest to your view of climate change?
items.scope: Changes in the Earth's average temperature over recent decades.
options: Mostly caused by humans, and a serious threat
Mostly caused by humans, but a manageable problem
Partly human, partly natural, with uncertain effects
Mostly natural, not caused by humans

items.stem: Should pollution cleanup give extra priority to low-income and minority neighborhoods?
items.scope: Federal cleanup money and enforcement.
options: Yes, with a set share of funding for those areas
Prioritize the most polluted areas, whoever lives there

items.stem: For climate change, where should government money mainly go?
items.scope: Answer even if you doubt climate change matters much.

sides.label: Cut emissions
sides.text: Cutting emissions, even if less is spent protecting communities from floods and heat.

sides.label: Prepare for effects
sides.text: Protecting communities from floods and heat, even if emissions are cut more slowly.

items.stem: Should single-use plastic bags be banned or charged for in stores?
items.scope: Bags given out at checkout.
options: Allowed, with a fee per bag
Allowed, free, as each store chooses
